newsitem.title: USA: Wall St. seeks guidance in past, planets, football.
newsitem.headline: Wall St. seeks guidance in past, planets, football.

text.p: The number seven. The Super Bowl. A solar eclipse. The month of January.
In the coming days, Wall Street will receive signs that could be key predictors to the record bull stock market's future.
Or, maybe not.
Market soothsayers sweat over corporate profit reports, economic indicators and computer-driven charts.
But with the Dow Jones Industrial Average hitting record highs day after day, nervous traders, analysts and investors are also turning to the tea leaves for help.
"In this business you grab on to anything you can grab on to," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
It could be especially so this year, as several ominous historical signs greeted 1997.

According to data from the Hirsch Organisation, publisher of the Stock Trader's Almanac, of the nine years ending in the number seven this century, only two -- 1927 and 1967 -- provided sizable gains, and the rest were years Wall Street would rather forget, including the most recent version, 1987.
Years following back-to-back gains of at least 15 percent in stocks have also not been friendly to stock investors.
The market posted 15-percent-plus gains in pre-crash years of 1927 and 1928 as well as in 1985 and 1986, said Yale Hirsch of the Hirsch Organisation.
The Dow gained 33 percent in 1995 and 26 percent in 1996.
Some are also seeing bearish signs in the stars.

Henry Weingarten, managing director of the Astrologers Fund, which uses astrology to help guide investment decisions, said a solar eclipse on March 8 will release "a big amount of cosmic power" that will produce an event on or about March 11.
The event will send markets tumbling, Weingarten said. He declined to say what the event might be, adding only that "by then it will be obvious."
Weingarten has a six-month Dow target of 5,200, a 24 percent drop from Wednesday's close at 6,850. He is bullish on Japan, despite the sharp drop in that market so far this year.
But going in Wall Street bulls' favour is the so-called "January Barometer."
According to this indicator, if the Standard & Poor's 500 finished January higher, so it would for the year. If it ended the month lower, it would follow suit for the full year.
The S&P 500 is up over six percent so far this January, with only six trading days left in the month.

The barometer has accurately forecast the market's direction 41 out of the past 46 years, Hirsch said. And there have been no errors in odd years with new congresses in Washington, such as this year, he noted.

Technical analysts give added credence to the barometer because of its long track record and its foundation in market factors including investor sentiment toward Washington and the economy at the start of the year.

"If they were worried and thought that interest rates were going through the roof, they would not go charging into the equity markets" at the start of the year, said John Brooks, director of marketing at Notley Information Service, which provides technical analysis on global markets.
An indicator less closely tied to market factors is the so-called Super Bowl Predictor.

Some analysts say it is ludicrous to argue that the outcome of a game, which could be determined by a field goal attempt sailing wide of the mark, could somehow predict the direction of the world's benchmark stock market.
But others will point to the predictor's 90 percent track record. The gauge has correctly called the Dow's direction 27 out of the 30 times the Super Bowl has been played.

The theory holds that if a team from the old National Football League won the Super Bowl, the stock market would end the year higher. If a team from the old American Football League won, stock prices would fall.
Last year it was a moot point -- the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Dallas Cowboys, two old NFL teams, faced each other.
But this year the Green Bay Packers of the old NFL go up against the New England Patriots, originally the Boston Patriots, of the old AFL.
"It's an unequivocal test of the signal," said Bob Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisers, who has tracked the Super Bowl Predictor since 1979.
The Packers are 14-point favourites in Sunday's game.
